Given two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ we know that the dot product can be computed using the formula

$$
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cdot |\,\mathbf{b}\,| \cdot \cos\theta,
$$

where $\theta$ is the angle formed between the vectors when their tails are placed at the same point.

However, there is another formula for the dot product that we can use if the two vectors are given in component form. If the components of our two vectors are

$$
\mathbf{a} = \langle {\color{red}a_x},{\color{blue}a_y}, a_z \rangle,
	\qquad
	\mathbf{b} = \langle {\color{red}b_x},{\color{blue}b_y}, b_z \rangle,
$$

then the dot product can be computed by summing up the products of corresponding components:

$$
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = {\color{red}a_x} \cdot {\color{red}b_x} + {\color{blue}a_y} \cdot  {\color{blue}b_y} + a_z \cdot b_z
$$

For example, if we have two vectors 

$$
\mathbf{a} = \langle {\color{red}3},{\color{blue}-5},2 \rangle,
	\qquad
	\mathbf{b} = \langle {\color{red}4},{\color{blue}6},7 \rangle,
$$

Then we can find the dot product of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =3\cdot 4+(-5)\cdot 6+2\cdot 7 \\  & =12-30+14 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** The procedure for computing the dot product works for vectors of any number of components. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3,-5⟩\cdot ⟨4,6⟩ & =3\cdot 4+(-5)\cdot 6 \\  & =12-30 \\  & =-18\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3,-5,2,1⟩\cdot ⟨4,6,7,9⟩ & =3\cdot 4+(-5)\cdot 6+2\cdot 7+1\cdot 9 \\  & =12-30+14+9 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

cas.before:
To understand the reasoning behind the formula for the dot product of two vectors, it's helpful to write the two vectors in terms of their elementary unit vectors and carry out the computation the long way.

For example, suppose we want to find the dot product $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$ for $\mathbf{a} = \langle 3,-5 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle 4,6 \rangle.$

Expressing the vectors in terms of their elementary unit vectors, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a=3i-5j,\,b=4i+6j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using properties of the dot product we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =(3i+(-5)j)\cdot (4i+6j) \\  & =(3\cdot 4)i\cdot i+(3\cdot 6)i\cdot j+(-5\cdot 4)j\cdot i+(-5\cdot 6)j\cdot j.\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}$ are perpendicular, meaning the angle between them is $\theta=90^\circ$ and consequently their dot product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}i\cdot j & =|\,i\,|\cdot |\,j\,|\cdot \operatorname{cos}{90}^{∘} \\  & =1\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, since the angle between a vector and itself is $\theta=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}i\cdot i & =|\,i\,|\cdot |\,i\,|\cdot \operatorname{cos}{0}^{∘} \\  & =1\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}j\cdot j & =|\,j\,|\cdot |\,j\,|\cdot \operatorname{cos}{0}^{∘} \\  & =1\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}i\cdot j & =j\cdot i=0, \\ i\cdot i & =j\cdot j=1,\end{aligned}
$$

and our computation reduces to

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =(3\cdot 4)\overbrace{i\cdot i}^{=1}+(3\cdot 6)\overbrace{i\cdot j}^{=0}+(-5\cdot 4)\overbrace{j\cdot i}^{=0}+(-5\cdot 6)\overbrace{j\cdot j}^{=1} \\  & =(3\cdot 4)\cdot 1+(3\cdot 6)\cdot 0+(-5\cdot 4)\cdot 0+(-5\cdot 6)\cdot 1 \\  & =(3\cdot 4)+(-5\cdot 6).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =⟨3,-5⟩\cdot ⟨4,6⟩ \\  & =(3\cdot 4)+(-5\cdot 6).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\times b\,| & =|\,a\,||\,b\,|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =7\cdot 6\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘} \\  & =7\cdot 6\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =21\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the magnitude of the cross product represents the area of the parallelogram spanned by the vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ as shown in the picture below.

cas.before:
The **scalar projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the distance that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

To illustrate the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ along $\mathbf{b},$ consider the point $P$ on the line that contains $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/fd/fd37bdb2a97b4125fb360990d3c4a36b48bcb50433de033a154799db00e474dd.png)

The length $OP$ is called the **scalar projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ (or the **component** of $\mathbf{a}$ along $\mathbf{b}$). It is denoted as $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and we can compute it using cosine in $\triangle OPA$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =OP \\  & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This formula is the general definition of the scalar projection:

$$
\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta
$$

$$
\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}= |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta
$$

However, sometimes we are not given the angle between two vectors. In such cases, we can solve for $\cos \theta$ in terms of the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =|\,a\,|\cdot \frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,|\,|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, another general formula for the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

The scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ can be negative. This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/c1/c19648ea2df1935e89e10df2f7f5ab33ad537a5fdb52bb97c3555c9a0365701e.png)

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2, \qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Notice that the angle $\theta$ between the vectors is obtuse. 

Computing the scalar projection of $\mathbf a$ onto $\mathbf b$ using the formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot \left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if $90^\circ < \theta \leq 180^\circ,$ then $\cos\theta <0$ and the scalar projection will be negative.

Given a level curve $f(x,y) = f(x_0,y_0),$ a **tangent vector** is

$$
\mathbf t(x_0,y_0) = f_y(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf j.
$$

 

To understand why the above vector is tangent to the level curve, first recall that the gradient vector $\nabla f(x_0,y_0)$ is normal to the level curve. Now, by computing the dot product, we see that the vector $\mathbf t$ is orthogonal to the gradient vector $\nabla\! f{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f\cdot t & =({f}_{x}\text{ }i+{f}_{y}\text{ }j)\cdot ({f}_{y}\text{ }i-{f}_{x}j) \\  & ={f}_{x}{f}_{y}-{f}_{y}{f}_{x} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $\mathbf t$ is tangent to the level curve.

cas.before:
Let's apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals to evaluate

$$
\int_C \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},
$$

where $f(x,y) = x^2y^3$ and $C$ is the path along the curve $y=x^2$ for $x \in [0,2].$ 

First, we must parameterize the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, \: t^2\right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of $C$ are given by

$$
\mathbf{r}(0)	= \left\langle 0, 0\right\rangle, \qquad
\mathbf{r}(2)	= \left\langle 2, 4\right\rangle.
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the path's endpoints defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(2,4).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(2))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(2,4)-f(0,0) \\  & ={2}^{2}\cdot {4}^{3}-{0}^{2}\cdot {0}^{3} \\  & =4\cdot 64 \\  & =256.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice how much faster it is to evaluate a line integral when we can use the fundamental theorem.

Here, we prove the fundamental theorem of line integrals in the two-dimensional case. The three-dimensional case is similar.

Let $C$ be a smooth curve $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and suppose that $f(x,y)$ is a differentiable function of two variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ We wish to show that

$$
\int_C \nabla f \cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

Using our usual formula for calculating line integrals, we can write the left-hand side as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}∇f\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the chain rule, the integrand above is simply the derivative of $f(\mathbf r(t))$ with respect to $t.$ Thus, we can write this integral as

$$
\int_a^b \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t}(f(\mathbf r(t)))\,\textrm d t.
$$

Finally, by the fundamental theorem of calculus, this is equal to 

$$
f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

This concludes the proof in the case where $C$ is smooth. It's easy to show that the theorem also holds for piecewise smooth curves.

cas.before:
Calculating the circulation of a vector field along a closed, piecewise smooth curve $C$ can be time-consuming because it often requires splitting $C$ into several parts, evaluating a line integral along each one, and calculating their sum. 

However, in such cases, we can often use Stokes' theorem to reduce the amount of work required by converting this sum of line integrals to a single surface integral. 

For example, suppose that $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2 + y^2$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x = \pm 1$ and $y=\pm 1.$ Suppose also that $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and 

$$
\mathbf{F} = \bigg\langle 0, \: \dfrac{1}{2}z^2, \: xz \bigg\rangle.
$$

Let's use Stokes' theorem to find the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C$.

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the curl of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} 
= 
{\left| \begin{array}{ccc}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial }{\partial  x}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial }{\partial  y}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial }{\partial  z}} \\ 0 & {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} {z}^{2} & x z\end{array} \right|}
=
\langle -z, -z, 0 \rangle.
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-z,\,-z,\,0⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{P},\,\underbrace{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{Q},\,\underbrace{0}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr & ={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2x+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2y+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/dc/dcf7ba14ac2c0f3da12efed6d539817ab1708273f5e8e665fdde14fee28bb4e3.png)

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
2\int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-1}^{1} x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 + y^3 \: \textrm{d}y  \: \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = 0.
$$

**Note**: Stokes theorem tells us that 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

 depends only on the circulation of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary of $S.$ Therefore, we could have evaluated our line integral by selecting *any* surface with $C$ as its bounding curve and integrating $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ over this surface.

Consider the surface integral of the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2+z^2
$$

 
over the parametric surface $S,$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u, \: 2v, \: -u \big\rangle, \quad (u,v)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is the unit square in the $uv$-plane given by

$$
D = \{(u,v) \: | \: 0\leq u\leq 1,\: 0\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

Let's compute the surface integral of $f$ over $S.$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the surface integral of $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x=u\,y=2v\,z=-u} \\  & ={u}^{2}+(2v)^{2}+(-u)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}+{u}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+8\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that  if $f(x,y)$ is a function whose partial derivatives

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y},
$$

exist and are continuous at a point $(x_0,y_0) \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the gradient of $f$ evaluated at $(x_0, y_0)$ is given by

 

$$
\nabla f(x_0,y_0) = \dfrac{\partial f }{\partial x}(x_0, y_0) \,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial f }{\partial y} (x_0, y_0)\,\mathbf{j} \, .
$$

 

Now suppose that the gradient vector exists at every point $(x,y)$ contained within the set $U\subset \mathbb R^2.$ Then, the **gradient vector field** of $f$ is defined as the map

$$
(x,y) \longmapsto \nabla f(x,y), \qquad (x,y)\in U.
$$

As an example, consider the function $f(x,y)=x^2-y^2.$ To find the gradient vector field of $f,$ we proceed as follows.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =2x\,i-2y\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

A sketch of this vector field is shown below.

![](images/74/7437bd110810a0356a25afea897634c152b0441aee8e6403aa051dd2c1f205a7.png)

Recall that the line integral with respect to arc length of a function $f(x,y)$ along a curve $C$ is given by

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_{t_a}^{t_b}  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

 

where $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t_a \leq  t \leq t_b$ is a parametrization of the curve $C.$

In this lesson, we will consider the case when the curve $C$ is a line segment. To calculate a line integral along a segment, we first need to parameterize the segment.

For example, suppose we wish to parameterize the segment between the points $A$ and $B$ with position vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ respectively, as shown below.

![](images/a4/a4d8d4e764dc4d7b29d5871d989100f2bb13b97aa4d034052037de4599d39e0e.png)

The vector equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ and passes through $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r=a+tv,\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf v$ is parallel to the line.

Let $\psi(x,y)$ be a two-variable function defined on a simply connected open set $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2.$ We know that for a point $(x_0,y_0)\in D,$ the vector

$$
\left.\left(\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}\,\mathbf i -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}\,\mathbf j\right)\right|_{(x_0,y_0)}
$$

is *tangential* to the level curve $\psi(x,y) = \psi(x_0,y_0).$ 

By computing this tangent vector at *every* point, we can generate a vector *field* tangential to the level curves of $\psi$ at every point.

With that in mind, let 

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)= P(x,y)\,\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf{j}
$$

 

be a vector field defined on $D.$ A function $\psi(x,y)$ is said to be a **stream function** of $\mathbf F$ if it satisfies

$$
P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad 
Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.
$$

For example, let's consider the function 

$$
\psi(x,y) = x^2+y^2.
$$

To construct a vector field with this stream function, we first compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{∂ψ}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =2y, \\ Q & =-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x} \\  & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the vector field with the stream function $\psi$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y) & =P\,i+Q\,j=2y\,i-2x\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

 

A diagram showing the surface $z = \psi(x,y),$ its level curves, and the vector field $\mathbf F$ are shown below.

![](images/69/696e6c623dbc3ecfae2643a7317d3d176294624289ecf6efb16debdc947d0394.png)

Note the following:

- The level curves of $\psi(x,y)$ are circles of the form $x^2+y^2=c$, and the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ in the $xy$-plane is tangential to these level curves.

- Suppose $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity of a fluid in the $xy$-plane. Then, the level curves of $\psi(x,y)$ represent the path of a massless particle in the $xy$-plane moving with the flow. For this reason, the level curves of $\psi$ are called **streamlines.**

- The stream function of a vector field is typically not unique since we can add any constant to $\psi$ to generate another valid stream function.

If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

 

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$

Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry.

To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png)

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png)

Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

This is easy to verify, since, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ 

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
=
-\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

Recall that the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F$ across a smooth, orientable surface $S$ with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ is given by 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot {\color{blue}\mathbf{n}} \,\textrm{d}S,
$$

where ${\color{blue}\mathbf{n}}$ is a unit normal vector that defines the orientation of the surface.

![](images/9a/9aa63a1e4f1d278cef6c53600e8fb9c60829de972ba7409afdc32837ecbc3e07.png)

If $S$ is given by a parametric equation of the form 

$$
\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}(u,v), \qquad (u,v)\in D\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,
$$

we can determine the unit normal vector using the fundamental product as follows:

$$
{\color{blue}\mathbf{n}} = \dfrac{\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v}{\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \|}
$$

$$

cas.before:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =-2 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(12+6)-1(-4-0) \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-v,\,y(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+v,\,z(u,v,w)={e}^{w}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{w}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{w}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 \\ 2u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}(2u+2u) \\  & =4u{e}^{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 4u{e}^{w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane.

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=u$ and $x-y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{4}-x+y=0\,⟹\,(x+y)^{4}-(x-y)=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

Now, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=u \\ x-y &=v\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,y=\frac{u-v}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this value into the equation of the given line yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\, & ⟹\,\frac{u-v}{2}=0\,⟹\,v=u\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &={u}^{4} \\ v &=u\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}(u-1) &=0 \\ v &=u.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{4}\le v\le u\}.
$$

![](images/1e/1ed905e319e689d3fc7955a30f58e0f3ae2e7a751c27b80201d2b43f58b4206c.png)

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(-2)^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{u}^{4}}^{u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[v]_{{u}^{4}}^{u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(u-{u}^{4})du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{u}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3}{10}\right) \\  & =\frac{3}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r
= \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \sin (\pi t), \qquad
y = \cos (\pi t), \qquad
z = t(2-t) = 2t-t^2.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j+z\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+(2t-{t}^{2})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2(1-t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+(2t-{t}^{2})\,k\,)\cdot (\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2(1-t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+(2t-{t}^{2})\cdot 2(1-t) \\  & =\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2(2t-{t}^{2})(1-t) \\  & =\pi ({cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t))+2(2t-3{t}^{2}+{t}^{3}) \\  & =\pi +4t-6{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\pi +4t-6{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\pi t+2{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[2\pi +8-16+8]-[0] \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Remember that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

- If the force works *against* the motion  of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.
$$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0
$$ is false, while statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ is true. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/20/20121d30445c9e756f1c2c024713bc6cd6f0464cfcfc24df68bc30c766c4988e.png)

 
So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ is true. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/0f/0ff98536c275458d68deabda91f56bf63e7c8f59f5ea79c68292332d8cd58d4f.png)

So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0;
$$ $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ only.

If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement “The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive” is false, while statement “The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero” is true. From the diagram below we see that $F$ acts perpendicular to $n$ at every point on $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $F$ through $C.$

![](images/d7/d7a469a331a3cda238fcefb9e7163743483975c4ecc7b962d6d5f8d79736693c.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

- Statement “The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is negative” is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/29/29f144d6f3ce8233a034025fe933bc57dbea5476c50a259853a98bd2a2b3a47b.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero” only.

cas.before:
A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$ has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0+0=0
$$

- Vector field $F(x,y)=xy\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=y+2y\ne 0.
$$

- Vector field $F(x,y)=2x\,i-y\,j$ doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2+(-1)\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$ only.

cas.before:
The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.
. 

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i-2xy\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-2xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+(-2x)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}={x}^{2},\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2xy.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y.
$$

Finally, we find the level curve of the stream function $ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ that passes through $P.$
First, we find the value of the stream function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(-1,-1) & =(-1)^{2}\cdot (-1) \\  & =1\cdot (-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,-1)$ is the $-1$-level curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}y & =-1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,-1)$ is $y=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.$
The vector field and the streamline through the point $P$ are shown below.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\mathbf{T}: {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v\end{array} \right]} 
\longrightarrow 
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( u , v ) \\ y ( u , v )\end{array} \right]}
$$

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \:  \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y) =  (2x+y)y^2
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x+y,
\qquad
v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

$$
\mathbf{T}^{-1}:{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]} \to {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u ( x , y ) \\ v ( x , y )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(\frac{3}{2},0) & =(2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+0,0) \\  & =(3,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(\frac{5}{2},0) & =(2\cdot \frac{5}{2}+0,0) \\  & =(5,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,3) & =(2\cdot 1+3,3) \\  & =(5,3) \\ {T}^{-1}(0,3) & =(2\cdot 0+3,3) \\  & =(3,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 3 \leq u \leq 5, \quad 0 \leq v \leq 3 \big\}
$$

![](images/c2/c296b1ee0451686608ec4b06c29d114ff1918233886d8471d3b2c118851aa25e.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} =\dfrac12
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral.

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y){y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{3}^{5}u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{3}^{5}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{3}^{5}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9\cdot 8 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$

$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2x+y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=2x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(0,1) & =(0+1,2(0)+1) \\  & =(1,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(1+0,2(1)+0) \\  & =(1,2) \\ {T}^{-1}(-1,3) & =(-1+3,2(-1)+3) \\  & =(2,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(0,2) & =(0+2,2(0)+2) \\  & =(2,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 2}
$$

![](images/3a/3a831bbc56c0ce5e749fcf45bd65825f297d7732158b8f9e371f2178e61b92c0.png)

$$

$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & \text{ }\text{ }0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{1+(x-y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,|-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,du]dv \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{2}du]dv \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}[u]_{0}^{2}\,dv \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,dv \\  & =2[\operatorname{arctan}⁡v]_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C.$ One such surface is our top (tilted) surface ${S}_{T}$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=4-x-y.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-x-y)=-1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-x-y)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨2xy,\,2z-{y}^{2},\,2y⟩{|}_{z=4-x-y} \\  & =⟨2xy,\,2(4-x-y)-{y}^{2},\,2y⟩ \\  & =⟨\underbrace{2xy}_{P},\,\underbrace{8-2x-2y-{y}^{2}}_{Q},\,\underbrace{2y}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{T}}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(2xy)\cdot (-1)-(8-2x-2y-{y}^{2})\cdot (-1)+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-2x-{y}^{2}+8)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/d0/d0f9cb64d0ae1c3615df5a05c9f580bb9c74f6529efd732cfd83e1f4328ff8a3.png)

cas.before:
A connected region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ can be contracted to a point.

![](images/7d/7d6aea1a62fb290702630ef95ec86f4119e7c8fdd74b8148b62b66e5ac871b58.png)

A connected *plane* region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ encloses only points in $D.$ In other words, the region does not contain any holes. Plane regions containing holes are not simply connected, since some simple closed curves cannot be contracted to a point:

![](images/c3/c3c3e7a60ff0dd917cf6c0b293dae7510e457a0455629add1c54cadac65248b7.png)

Let's now examine our regions in turn.

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1}$ is *not* simply connected. The region contains all the points of ${R}^{2}$ except those on the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ Thus, the region is formed by two disjoint pieces and, therefore, is not even a connected region.

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,(x,y)\ne (0,0)}$ is *not* simply connected since it's a plane region with a hole at $(0,0).$

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,x\ge 0}$ is simply connected. It's a plane region without holes.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,x\ge 0}$ only.

cas.before:
A connected region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ can be contracted to a point.

![](images/7d/7d6aea1a62fb290702630ef95ec86f4119e7c8fdd74b8148b62b66e5ac871b58.png)

A connected *plane* region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ encloses only points in $D.$ In other words, the region does not contain any holes. Plane regions containing holes are not simply connected, since some simple closed curves cannot be contracted to a point:

![](images/c3/c3c3e7a60ff0dd917cf6c0b293dae7510e457a0455629add1c54cadac65248b7.png)

Let's now examine our regions in turn.

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,y-x\ge 0}$ is simply connected. Indeed, it is the half-plane $y\ge x.$ So,   it's a plane region without holes,

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1}$ is *not* simply connected since it's a plane region with a hole (containing all points of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1$).

- Region ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,y+x\ne 0}$ is *not* simply connected. The region contains all the points of ${R}^{2}$ except those on the straight line $y=-x.$ Thus, the region is formed by two disjoint half-planes and, therefore, is not even a connected region.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,y-x\ge 0}$ only.

cas.before:
Remember that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.
$$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0
$$ is false, while statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0
$$ is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$  works against the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B.$

![](images/14/14e94a2c5d0faabff1beeadeccb6999aa2edd71fce06fff8a2655db74e585eba.png)

So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.
$$

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0
$$ is true. It's clear from the picture below that if we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves from $B$ to $A.$

![](images/c5/c54487081f2150216b7e41b1351f0f7b19c794b140297789f19d9afe830bd7b1.png)

So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0;
$$ $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0
$$ only.

cas.before:
Remember that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

- If the force works *against* the motion  of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.
$$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0
$$ is false, while statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ is true. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/e0/e07fca985a11d4edb66ea91d9a560ab134d81f5f20aaba8b376677d0de2dd3e7.png)

 
So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0
$$ is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/78/78de6ce0133bec33c14eabb43db2e53eb8d76653aa1fc121c83f47c4b91c3b94.png)

 
So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ only.

cas.before:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/3b/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(x\,i+y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =2(2-(-2)) \\  & =2\cdot 4 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot 8=32.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =3 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot 3-1\cdot 2 \\  & =9-2 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

cas.before:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy-3{x}^{2}=-y \\ 2xy-3{x}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2xy-3{x}^{2}+y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-3{x}^{2}+y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-3{x}^{2}+y)j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i-2(y-3x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j$, we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((2x+1)\,i-2(y-3x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -2(y-3x) & =0 \\ y & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=3x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy-3{x}^{2}+y & =0 \\ 2x(3x)-3{x}^{2}+3x & =0 \\ 6{x}^{2}-3{x}^{2}+3x & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}+3x & =0 \\ 3x(x+1) & =0 \\ x & =0\,\text{or}\,x=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=0$, we get $y=0$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=-3$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,-3).$

$$

$$

$$

And we substitute $v=xy$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & xy=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & xy=3\,⟹\,v=2\end{aligned}
$$

The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.
. 

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

Finally, we find the level curve of the stream function $ψ(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ that passes through $P.$
First, we find the value of the stream function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(0,\pi ) & ={e}^{(0)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the streamline that passes through $P(0,\pi )$ is the $0$-level curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our possible streamlines are $y=k\pi $ for any integer $k.$ The streamline that passes through $P(0,\pi )$ is $y=\pi .$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$ 

Note that the change of variables

$$
u={x}^{2}+y,\,v=2x+z,\,w=z,
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v,w)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,-1\le v\le 6,\,1\le w\le 4}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$ 

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2x & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(2-0) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$

First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2x & =2xy+2y-2 \\ {y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$  

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y)j \\  & =(2y-2x-2)\,i-(2-2y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2y-2x-2)\,i-(2-2y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2y-2x-2 & =0 \\ 2(y-x-1) & =0 \\ y & =x+1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2x-2xy-2y & =-2 \\ (x+1)^{2}+2x-2x(x+1)-2(x+1)+2 & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1)-2(x+1)+2(x+1) & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1)-\cancel{2(x+1)}+\cancel{2(x+1)} & =0 \\ (x+1)^{2}-2x(x+1) & =0 \\ (x+1)(x+1-2x) & =0 \\ (x+1)(-x+1) & =0 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=1$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(1,2).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=0$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,0).$

cas.before:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=\frac{{0}^{2}}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement “The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$” is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+(x)^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The limit evaluates to $1$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$” is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{({x}^{2})}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{4}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{2})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+0} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The limit exists and is equal to $1$” is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

cas.before:
The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that 

$$
F(x,y)=2xi-2y\,j
$$

 is a vector field with simply connected domain $D,$ where $P(x,y)=2x$ and $Q(x,y)=-2y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2-2=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=2x,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)=2xy+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)=2xy+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)=2xy.
$$

Finally, we find the level curves of the stream function $ψ(x,y)=2xy$ given by the equations $ψ(x,y)=c.$

Notice that the range of $ψ(x,y)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, we will consider level curves for any value of $c.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =c \\ 2xy & =c \\ y & =\frac{c}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives us a family of hyperbolas with asymptotes $y=0$ and $x=0$ and, for $c=0,$ the lines $y=0$ and $x=0.$ Therefore, the correct graph (along with the vector field $F$) is as follows:

cas.before:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,u⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨3x,\,3y,\,z⟩{|}_{x=u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,y=u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\,z={u}^{2}} \\  & =⟨3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,{u}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,{u}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,u⟩ \\  & =3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v)+3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot (-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v)+{u}^{2}\cdot u \\  & =-6{u}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v)+{u}^{3} \\  & =-5{u}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,-5{u}^{3}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\right)=\frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\right)=\frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=1/({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{x}_{P},\,\underbrace{y}_{Q},\,\underbrace{-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y\,i-2x{y}^{2}\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=-2x{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=4xy+(-4xy)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}=(xy)^{2}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
v=16.
$$

$$

Note that the length of the altitude (height) can be related to the area of the triangle as follows:

$$
A_{\bigtriangleup} = \dfrac{b \cdot h}{2},
$$

 
where $b$ is a base and $h$ is the corresponding altitude of the triangle.

For the $\bigtriangleup\!ABC,$ we have $h=CH,$ and $b=AB.$ So, we have

$$
A_{\bigtriangleup} = \dfrac{1}{2} CH \cdot AB.
$$

So, to find $CH,$ we first find $A_{\bigtriangleup}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(i+j+2k)-(-i+j) \\  & =2i+2k \\  & =⟨2,0,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(i-j+k)-(-i+j) \\  & =2i-2j+k \\  & =⟨2,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\times \overset{\to }{AC} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =(0\cdot 1-2\cdot (-2))i-(2\cdot 1-2\cdot 2)j+(2\cdot (-2)-0\cdot 2)k \\  & =4i+2j-4k \\  & =⟨4,2,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{AB}\times \overset{\to }{AC}| \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $\bigtriangleup\!ABC$ is

$$
A_{\bigtriangleup} = \dfrac{1}{2}A = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 6 = 3.
$$

Let's also compute $AB$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =|\overset{\to }{AB}| \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}CH\cdot AB \\ 3 & =\frac{1}{2}CH\cdot 2\sqrt{2} \\ 3 & =CH\cdot \sqrt{2} \\ CH & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ CH & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+3y,\,v=z-3y,\,w=z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le u\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le w\le 2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-3-0) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
